subject: English
topic: Sentence Improvement — Identifying Correct Alternatives (W11 B2)

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'She is working here since 2018.'
(A) She has been working here
(B) She was working here
(C) She had been working here
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Since 2018' signals a period starting in the past and continuing to the present. This requires the PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS tense: 'has been working'. 'Is working' (simple present continuous) is wrong with 'since' — it implies only the current moment. 'Was working' = past continuous (action finished in the past). 'Had been working' = past perfect continuous (requires another past reference point). Rule: 'since' + point of time → has/have been + V-ing.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'He is a man of few words but his suggestions are always worth to consider.'
(A) worth considering
(B) worth to be considered
(C) worthy considering
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Worth' functions as a preposition and takes a gerund (V-ing), never an infinitive. Correct: 'worth considering' (not 'worth to consider'). The pattern is: worth + gerund. Examples: 'worth reading', 'worth trying', 'worth visiting'. 'Worth to be considered' adds a passive infinitive unnecessarily. 'Worthy' would need 'of' + gerund: 'worthy of consideration'. Most natural/correct: 'worth considering'.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'Neither of the two options are acceptable.'
(A) is acceptable
(B) were acceptable
(C) will be acceptable
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Neither' (used alone or with 'of') takes a SINGULAR verb: 'Neither of the two options IS acceptable.' The word 'neither' is grammatically singular even though it refers to two items. Rule: Neither = not one and not the other = singular. Compare: 'Neither plan is feasible.' Trap: students match the plural noun 'options' with 'are', but the subject is 'neither' (singular), not 'options'. Same rule applies to 'either'.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'The report was submitted by him on time, wasn't he?'
(A) wasn't it?
(B) was it?
(C) didn't he?
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. In a question tag, the subject of the tag must match the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT of the main clause. The main clause 'The report was submitted...' has 'the report' as its grammatical subject. Subject = 'the report' = it. So the tag = 'wasn't it?' (not 'wasn't he?', which wrongly uses 'he' from the phrase 'by him'). Rule: The tag pronoun refers to the subject of the sentence, not to other nouns in the sentence. 'was it?' = wrong polarity (affirmative sentence needs negative tag).

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'Despite of working hard, he failed the examination.'
(A) Despite working hard
(B) In despite of working hard
(C) Despite having worked hard
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Despite' is a preposition and does NOT take 'of' after it. Correct: 'Despite working hard'. Compare: 'In spite OF working hard' (in spite OF = correct). Students confuse 'despite' with 'in spite of' and wrongly add 'of' after 'despite'. Option C ('Despite having worked hard') is grammatically possible in some contexts but adds an unnecessary perfect aspect here; A is simpler and standard. Rule: despite + noun/gerund (no 'of'); in spite of + noun/gerund (with 'of').

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'One of the best novels that has been written in this century is by Amitav Ghosh.'
(A) have been written
(B) were written
(C) was written
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. The structure is 'one of the best novels THAT have been written'. The relative pronoun 'that' refers to 'novels' (plural), not 'one' (singular). Rule: 'One of those/the [plural noun] that/who + PLURAL VERB'. So 'that have been written' is correct. 'Has been written' wrongly treats 'that' as referring to 'one' (singular). This is the classic SSC 'one of those who' trap — the verb after the relative clause agrees with the PLURAL NOUN, not with 'one'.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'He said that he will come tomorrow.'
(A) he would come the next day
(B) he will come the next day
(C) he would come tomorrow
(D) No improvement

options.option_text: he would come the next day
he will come the next day

questions.explanation: A is correct. Reported speech (indirect speech) changes: (1) 'will' → 'would' (modal backshift in past reported speech). (2) 'tomorrow' → 'the next day' (time expression changes when the reporting verb is in past tense). Both changes must apply: 'He said that he WOULD come THE NEXT DAY.' Option B keeps 'will' (wrong — no backshift). Option C changes 'will' to 'would' but keeps 'tomorrow' (wrong — 'tomorrow' refers to a day relative to the reporting moment, which no longer applies in indirect speech).

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'Between you and I, the plan is flawed.'
(A) Between you and me
(B) Among you and I
(C) Between you and myself
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Between' is a preposition. A preposition must be followed by an OBJECT pronoun, not a subject pronoun. Object form of 'I' = 'me'. Correct: 'Between you and ME'. 'Between you and I' is a hypercorrection (people avoid 'me' thinking it sounds uneducated, but after a preposition 'me' is grammatically required). 'Myself' is reflexive/emphatic; it cannot replace 'me' after a preposition unless there is a reflexive antecedent. Rule: between/for/to/from/with/by + me (not 'I' or 'myself').

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'The committee have decided to postpone the meeting.'
(A) has decided
(B) have all decided
(C) had decided
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. When a collective noun (committee, jury, team, government) acts as a SINGLE UNIT making ONE decision, it takes a SINGULAR verb in standard Indian/formal English usage. 'The committee HAS decided' = the committee as a body decided (one decision). Compare: 'The committee are divided in their opinions' = singular decision vs. divided individual actions (British English allows plural for divided action). In SSC standard usage, 'committee' + single action = singular verb 'has'. Note: British English sometimes uses plural for collectives, but SSC follows the standard/Indian convention.

questions.stem:
Improve the underlined part: 'He runs quick to catch the bus every morning.'
(A) runs quickly
(B) runs more quicker
(C) runs quickest
(D) No improvement
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Quick' is an adjective; it should not modify a verb ('runs'). The correct form is the adverb 'QUICKLY' to modify the verb 'runs'. Rule: adjectives modify nouns/pronouns; adverbs modify verbs/adjectives/other adverbs. 'Runs quickly' = correct. 'More quicker' is a double comparative (grammatically wrong). 'Quickest' is superlative (not needed here). Common SSC trap: using adjectives where adverbs are required ('drive careful' should be 'drive carefully').
